There aren’t many ways to experience the ancient world. We can learn its languages, at least the ones that have left behind decipherable writings; we can behold its artifacts; we can visit its ruins. But nothing gets us quite as close to entering the consciousness of our distant forebears as hearing the music — or at least the sounds — that they did. In the new Archaeologist’s Notebook video above, Giselle Király gives us a tour through ancient musical history, explaining the instruments of those times that survive in one form or another today. That tour begins at a much earlier point than many would expect: 40,000 years ago, in the depths of the last Ice Age, when humans were already punctuating their struggle for survival with organized sound.

As evidence, Király points to the “tiny, exquisitely crafted flutes carved from animal bone and mammoth ivory” discovered on cave floors around Europe. Surprisingly, when played in replica form, these vulture- or swan-bone flutes actually sound somewhat Middle Eastern. But whatever the stylistic traits of the music their original players produced, that music had the potential to confer benefits beyond immediate pleasure: “It would’ve connected people, built cohesion within the community,” and maybe even bridged “the land of the living with some spiritual world.” Each of the other discovered or reconstructed instruments, like swingable “bullroarers,” bone rasps, and lithophones (of the kind previously featured here on Open Culture) would have played its own sonic part to that end.

Király also discusses the lavishly decorated Lyres of Ur, the world’s oldest surviving stringed instruments; a 3,500-year-old Egyptian long-necked lute with a guitar-like fingerboard; and a set of 65 Chinese bianzhong bells covering a five-octave range. But music isn’t just about the objects it’s played with. Also important are the means of recording it, an ancient example of which Király cites in the Hurrian Hymn to Nikkal inscribed on a clay tablet around 1400 BC, the oldest known complete musical notation. Centuries later, in the Greek-speaking world — and in the more monumental form of a marble stele — a man named Seikilos recorded an epitaph to which we now refer by his name. The lyrics of this oldest completely preserved, fully playable musical composition exhort the listener: “While you live, shine. Have no grief at all.” For “life exists only for a short while,” and “time demands its toll.” The ancients needed to hear this no less, perhaps, than we do.
